routes.description: Establish that neither determined nor undetermined action gives agents the ultimate authorship required for philosophical free will.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actions arise from force or unchosen wants whose causal histories never terminate in self-created control, while explaining practical agency without ultimate desert.

motionBridge.description: Connect the absence of control over determining causes and desires to the conclusion that voluntary action lacks ultimate authorship.

centralBridges.description: Establish that determined events inherit prior causes while undetermined events are uncontrolled, leaving neither branch as agent-authored control.
Establish that conduct follows either force or motivating wants and that agents do not independently choose the wants governing action.
Trace character and choice through upbringing, genetics, circumstances, and dispositions without reaching a self-created source.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how deterrence, prevention, rehabilitation, and compassion remain available without attributing ultimate moral desert.
Account for moral motivation and social restraint through causally formed desires rather than an independently chosen will.

routes.description: Establish that determined agents can possess meaningful freedom when conduct belongs to them, is voluntary, and lacks relevant coercive constraints.
routes.successCriteria: Show that freedom need not require ultimate self-creation, that voluntary agency admits context-sensitive degrees, and that causal description does not exhaust personal or ethical meaning.

motionBridge.description: Connect attributable, voluntary, and substantially unconstrained conduct to a defensible form of freedom despite causal determination.

centralBridges.description: Preserve a meaningful distinction between compelled conduct and action attributable to the person as its relevant source.
Explain freedom and its absence through degrees of voluntary control and context-sensitive impediments rather than causation alone.
Establish that interpersonal responsibility and first-person agency contain semantic and ethical dimensions not exhausted by third-person causal description.
Show how action may genuinely belong to a person while also arising through processes that the person did not deliberately manufacture.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support the nonreductive account by treating conscious understanding as temporally and socially constituted rather than a static internal object.
Preserve the richer normative meaning of moral intuition against reduction to psychological or evolutionary causation.

sectionSelections.title: Determination, randomness, and ultimate control
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion turns first on whether either causal determination or its absence can provide the kind of authorship required for free action.

proSelections.proposition: Free will requires genuine authorship and an ability to have acted differently, but neither randomness nor determination supplies the agent with the required control.
Neither God nor an immaterial soul escapes the determined-or-undetermined dilemma, so changing the substrate does not supply free control.

conSelections.proposition: Deterministic causation is compatible with free action because compelled conduct differs meaningfully from voluntary conduct whose cause is attributable to the agent.
Actions can genuinely belong to a person while also happening to that person, without requiring the person to have deliberately manufactured the underlying thought or desire.

sectionSelections.title: Unchosen desires and voluntary action
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue determines whether acting from one's own motives is enough for freedom or merely transmits causal factors the agent never selected.

proSelections.proposition: Every mental choice or desire is either uncontrolled randomness or part of a causal chain extending beyond the agent, so no such event provides ultimate control.
Agents may act as they want but cannot simply choose what they want, while action produced by force is plainly uncontrolled.

conSelections.proposition: Ordinary freedom concerns meaningful practices, absent constraints, and degrees of voluntary control rather than an abstract demand that desires themselves be chosen.
Freedom admits degrees, and ordinary voluntary actions can belong to an agent without arising from conscious deliberation or an explicitly willed decision.

sectionSelections.title: Causal sourcehood and first-person agency
sectionSelections.rationale: The competing routes depend on whether causal histories exhaust agency or leave a first-person and personally attributable dimension of action intact.

proSelections.proposition: Human choices reflect unchosen upbringing, genetics, circumstances, and dispositions, so tracing responsibility backward never reaches a self-created source of agency.
A person can move voluntarily while remaining unable to identify how wanting or deciding produces the bodily movement.

conSelections.proposition: A prediction disclosed to a self-aware subject can provoke its own defeat, leaving a first-person perspective not captured by ordinary third-person causal prediction.
Conscious thought is socially and behaviorally constituted before private representation, so reductive inspection cannot isolate it as a discrete internal object.

sectionSelections.title: Responsibility, desert, and interpersonal ethics
sectionSelections.rationale: The consequences of each account depend on whether responsibility requires ultimate desert or can instead operate as a graded interpersonal and ethical practice.

proSelections.proposition: Rejecting ultimate moral desert still permits preventive, deterrent, and rehabilitative responses to criminal conduct.
Recognizing that wrongdoers did not control the factors determining their behavior can encourage compassion, forgiveness, and understanding.

conSelections.proposition: Responsibility is an ethically indispensable interpersonal practice, and freedom is better understood through nuanced recognition of persons than as an absolute metaphysical possession.
Ethical judgment should preserve tension between responsible choice and helpless determination instead of collapsing human agency into either extreme.

sectionSelections.title: Causal explanation and moral meaning
sectionSelections.rationale: This issue tests whether a causal account of moral motivation replaces normative agency or can coexist with the richer meanings used in ethical life.

proSelections.proposition: Moral motivation can be explained as an evolved emotional desire that competes with other desires and promotes stable cooperative societies.

conSelections.proposition: Psychological or evolutionary explanation of moral intuition does not eliminate or fully reduce its richer normative meaning.
